account: Shapiro et al. 2011 provides the theoretical grounding for the persistence and concurrent-update semantics of the question/answer substrate. The paper distinguishes state-based CRDTs (CvRDTs), where replicas merge full states via a least-upper-bound (LUB) operation over a monotonic semilattice, from operation-based CRDTs (CmRDTs), where replicas apply effect-updates that commute. Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC) demands that correct replicas that have delivered the same updates have equivalent state, without requiring rollback or consensus. Sufficient conditions for SEC are monotonicity in a semilattice (CvRDT) and commutativity of concurrent updates (CmRDT). Reusable concrete types include the add-only (grow-only) set, the U-Set (observed-remove set using tombstones — actually presented as add-only A plus tombstone R), the increment/decrement counter, and a directed-graph CRDT. Design inferences for the question/answer substrate: model questions, answers, and tags as add-only sets (or add-wins sets for tags) so that concurrent additions converge; derive a directed-graph-like structure for question-answer-answer links; and identify invariants CRDTs cannot enforce — uniqueness of canonical object IDs, schema validity, and tag-vocabulary control — which the runtime must enforce.
assumptions: The question/answer substrate is implemented as a replicated object or set of objects where each replica accepts updates locally without global synchronization, as assumed by the CRDT model.
The runtime can enforce invariants that CRDTs cannot, without violating the CRDT's convergence guarantee (e.g., via a separate validation layer before applying an update).

boundary_findings.alternative_explanation: The paper's graph semantics are intentionally permissive to support web-crawling scenarios; the substrate might choose the same semantics deliberately.
boundary_findings.consequence_if_absorbed: The substrate would permit arcs from answer objects to non-existent question objects, and these would be silently hidden by lookup until the target is created, which may hide legitimate concurrent additions or require non-trivial reconciliation with other CRDTs.
boundary_findings.narrative: The Shapiro paper's directed-graph example requires head-vertex existence as a precondition for addArc (i.e., a runtime-enforced invariant), but the same paper's add-only set and U-Set do not have such structural preconditions. If the substrate adopts the graph semantics without a runtime schema check, it could allow dangling arcs that the paper's lookup method would mask, potentially leading to invisible or inconsistent edges in the question/answer graph.
boundary_findings.smallest_suspected_scope: The substrate's link/edge data model for question-answer-answer relations.

citations.excerpt: An object is a tuple(S,s0,q,u,m). The replica at process pi has state si∈S... Method m serves to merge the state from a remote replica. (P3) ... an op-based object is a tuple (S,s0,q,t,u,P) ... an update is split into a pair(t,u), where t is a side-effect-free prepare-update method and u is an effect-update method. (P5)

claims.statement: Shapiro et al. define two replication styles: state-based objects (CvRDT) where an object is a tuple (S, s0, q, u, m) and merge method m merges remote state into local state, versus operation-based objects (CmRDT) with tuple (S, s0, q, t, u, P) where an update is split into a side-effect-free prepare-update t and effect-update u that executes at all replicas.

citations.excerpt: Strong Convergence: Correct replicas that have delivered the same updates have equivalent state: ∀i,j: ci=cj ⇒ si≡sj. (Definition 3)

claims.statement: Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC) is defined as Eventual Consistency plus Strong Convergence: correct replicas that have delivered the same updates have equivalent state, ∀i,j: ci=cj ⇒ si≡sj.

citations.excerpt: Deﬁnition 4 (Monotonic semilattice object): ... (i) Set S of payload values forms a semilattice ordered by ≤. (ii) Merging states with remote state s′ computes the LUB of the two states, i.e., s•m(s′)=s⊔s′. (iii) State is monotonically non-decreasing across updates, i.e., s≤s•u. Theorem 1 ... any state-based object that satisﬁes the monotonic semilattice property is SEC.

claims.statement: For state-based CRDTs, a sufficient condition for SEC is monotonicity in a semilattice: the payload set S forms a semilattice ordered by ≤; merging computes the LUB s•m(s′)=s⊔s′; and state is monotonically non-decreasing across updates.

citations.excerpt: Theorem 2 (Commutative Replicated Data Type (CmRDT)). Assuming causal delivery of updates and method termination, any op-based object that satisﬁes the commutativity property for all concurrent updates, and whose delivery precondition is satisﬁed by causal delivery, is SEC.

claims.statement: For operation-based CRDTs, a sufficient condition for SEC is that all concurrent updates commute; the paper's Theorem 2 states that an op-based object satisfying commutativity, with delivery precondition satisfied by causal delivery, is SEC.

citations.excerpt: Another simple CRDT construct is an add-only set object (S,⊆, ∅, value, add(e), ∪). ... It is well-known that sets ordered by ⊆ form a semi-lattice with ∪ as the LUB operator.

claims.statement: A concrete reusable CRDT is the add-only (grow-only) set: payload is a set, ordered by inclusion; update add(e) adds e; merge is union; this forms a semilattice with ∪ as LUB.

citations.excerpt: They propose a set with both add and remove operations by associating two add-only sets A and R; adding an element adds it to A, removing it adds it to R; query value() returns the set difference A\R. (P9) ... Fig. 3 ... update addVertex(vertex v) ... let w = unique() ... V := V ∪ {(v,w)}. (P11)

claims.statement: The paper presents a set with both add and remove (U-Set) built from two add-only sets A and R, where remove adds to the tombstone set R and value() returns A\R; it also presents an op-based directed-graph CRDT with addVertex/removeVertex/addArc/removeArc using unique tags.

citations.excerpt: add-only set ... is clearly monotonic ... Therefore, the add-only set is a CRDT.

claims.statement: Design inference: For the question/answer substrate, treat question objects, answer objects, and tag memberships as add-only sets (or add-wins sets for tags) so that concurrent additions converge under union, matching the CvRDT model.

citations.excerpt: note that addArc must work even if the page at the tail of the arc has not yet been found ... lookup of the corresponding arc should fail.

claims.statement: Design inference: Model the substrate's graph (question-answer-answer links) as a directed-graph CRDT with add-vertex/add-arc semantics, using unique IDs/tags per object so that adding an edge does not require its tail to already exist and concurrent additions converge.

citations.excerpt: A conﬂict is a combination of concurrent updates, which may be individually correct, but that, taken together, would violate some invariant. ... (paper discusses conflict arbitration elsewhere)

claims.statement: Design inference: CRDTs cannot enforce invariants such as uniqueness of a canonical question/answer/tag identifier, schema validity (e.g., a tag must be attached only to a valid object), or tag-vocabulary control (only pre-approved tags); these must be enforced by the runtime outside the CRDT merge logic.

counterevidence: The Shapiro paper does not explicitly discuss uniqueness, schema validity, or tag-vocabulary control as invariants; the paper only gives a graph example with preconditions on addArc requiring head existence, not on the tail.

The U-Set example in the paper uses tombstones but also assumes each element is unique and added only once; the paper explicitly notes this assumption, so the U-Set's convergence guarantee depends on the runtime enforcing uniqueness of elements.
next_observation: Review the Dung and social-influence papers for how to define conflict edges and staged visibility in a way compatible with CRDT merge semantics.
unresolved: The paper does not specify how to choose between add-wins and remove-wins semantics for sets; the choice must be made per use case (the paper notes multiple alternatives are possible).
The paper's graph CRDT example is op-based and relies on a causal, reliable broadcast; the substrate's communication layer must provide this to use the graph directly.
The paper's garbage-collection algorithm for logs is only live if no process is crashed; the substrate must define its own tombstone or GC policy for removed elements.
The paper does not address how to compose CRDTs with runtime-enforced invariants without breaking the monotonicity or commutativity conditions.
